description: The true path of the miniature: the carter's first tale against the narrator's own observation, and ruled out; his second, two statements, one of them needed and one against the cook's word with nothing confirmed to decide it; the curate, who shares nothing with the cook, agrees with her, and the carter's charge cannot stand.

moves.why: I looked into the forge at ten to nine myself: he was not there. What he first told me cannot be so.
And a man who says he never left the forge, when he did, has a reason to say so.

moves.see: someone had been in for it
moves.why: The lantern is kept in the counting-room. Someone had been in.
The door was locked when I came back.
And the key was on its nail: the bag went out by the key.
Something else from the same source is ruled out, so I do not take this on trust; but nothing speaks against this one, and I hold it likely.
He says himself that he had the key and went in. That goes against him, and I believe it.

moves.see: in her kitchen from eight till nine
moves.why: Mrs. Dabney has Mr. Wicks at her table the whole hour.
If she is right, Mr. Wicks did not go near the counting-room.
Mr. Lisle saw him there too, and Mr. Lisle has nothing to do with the mill or with Mrs. Dabney.
Two people who share nothing say the same of the same moment: I take it as confirmed.
So Mr. Wicks was not in the counting-room at half past eight. Tarrant has now told me two things that were not so.
It was Tarrant who put him in the counting-room.
The cook and the curate both have him there.
The bag went by the key, Tarrant had the key in that hour, and Mr. Wicks was at his supper.
He was in the kitchen across the yard.
